accroche: Count the passes made by the white team. One viewer in two will not see the gorilla cross the screen.
contenu_vulgarise:
A simple instruction: watch this video and count the passes made by the players in white shirts. A second team, in black, also moves around; ignore them.

In the middle of the sequence, a person in a gorilla suit walks into the frame, stops at the center, beats their chest, then walks off. They remain visible for several seconds.

About half of the viewers do not see them.

The rate varies with the difficulty of the instruction: the more attention the counting demands, for example if you have to tell direct passes from bounce passes, the more the gorilla disappears.

## What It Shows

Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris publish this experiment in 1999. The phenomenon has a name: inattentional blindness. We do not perceive what we are not looking for, even when it is perfectly visible, even at the center of our gaze.

But the essential point lies elsewhere. Those who did not see the gorilla almost always refuse to believe it. They are convinced that something like that would have jumped out at them, and the video has to be replayed before they give in.

We are therefore blind twice: to what we are not looking for, and to the very existence of this blind spot.

## It Is Not a Matter of Distraction

In 2013, Trafton Drew and his colleagues insert the image of a gorilla, much larger than a typical lung nodule, into a series of chest CT scans. They then ask experienced radiologists to look for nodules in them.

Eighty-three percent do not see the gorilla. Eye tracking shows, however, that most of them looked right at it.

Expertise does not immunize; it may rather make the phenomenon worse. A trained eye is a selective eye, and selection is precisely what manufactures the blind spot.

## What This Shifts

The result contradicts a very solid intuition: that of an eye that would record the whole scene, with attention then sorting through it. The opposite happens. Attention decides what is seen, and the rest never reaches consciousness.

This concerns testimony, driving, surveillance, medical diagnosis. And it ruins a sentence we utter without thinking: “I would have seen it.”

Not necessarily. And you would have no way of knowing.

The corollary is more useful than the finding itself. Since the blind spot is invisible from the inside, it is not corrected by promising to be more attentive. It is corrected by changing method: a second pair of eyes, a checklist, a protocol that forces you to look for what you do not expect.

repere.texte: In a series of chest CT scans into which the image of a gorilla had been inserted, 83% of experienced radiologists did not see it, even though eye tracking shows that most of them had looked right at it.

carte.punch: Count the passes. One viewer in two will not see the gorilla.
carte.idee: It crosses the screen at the center, stops, beats its chest. Half of people miss it, and refuse to believe it. Among radiologists looking for nodules, 83% missed a gorilla slipped into the scan that they had nonetheless looked right at.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The study on radiologists, with the eye-tracking maps.

quiz.question: What does the 2013 study of radiologists add?
choix: That the phenomenon disappears as soon as observers are warned in advance
That expertise does not protect: 83% missed a gorilla they had nonetheless looked right at
That experts detect the anomaly but choose not to report it
That inattentional blindness concerns only moving images
quiz.explication: The eye tracking is decisive: most radiologists had laid their eyes on the gorilla without seeing it. Expertise may even make the phenomenon worse, as a trained eye is a selective eye, and selection is what manufactures the blind spot. The effect also holds for still images.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What makes the rate of viewers who do not see the gorilla vary, in Simons and Chabris's original experiment?
choix: The rate depends only on the viewers' age, the youngest systematically missing it
The rate never varies, whatever the difficulty of the task requested
The rate varies with the difficulty of the instruction: the more attention the counting demands, the more the gorilla disappears
The rate decreases when the video is watched on a smaller screen
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The more attention the counting instruction demands, for example telling direct passes from bounce passes, the more likely the gorilla is to go unnoticed: it is the difficulty of the task that governs the detection rate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do most viewers who did not see the gorilla react when it is pointed out to them?
choix: They accept it immediately without showing the slightest surprise
They immediately accuse the experimenters of having rigged the video
They then recall having noticed a blurry silhouette, without certainty
They almost always refuse to believe it, and the video has to be replayed before they give in
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Convinced that something like that would have jumped out at them, those who did not see the gorilla almost always refuse to take it on faith, and the video has to be replayed before they give in: a blindness to the blind spot itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the text say inattentional blindness is effectively corrected, since promising to be attentive is not enough?
choix: By training for several months with intensive visual concentration exercises
By changing method: a second pair of eyes, a checklist, a protocol that looks for the unexpected
By consciously promising to be more attentive next time
By slowing down the speed at which the images observed scroll by
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Since the blind spot is invisible from the inside, promising to be more attentive is not enough: the text specifies that it is corrected by changing method, a second pair of eyes, a checklist, a protocol that forces you to look for the unexpected.
